title: How to Tell If a Source Is Credible Online
excerpt: A polished website can be wrong. A badly designed PDF can contain excellent research. A '.org' address can belong to an advocacy group, and a page with dozens of citations can still misrepresent what those citations say.
seoTitle: How to Tell If a Source Is Credible | Kahana
metaDescription: A credibility-checking method for websites, articles, statistics, and viral claims, based on lateral reading rather than surface-level trust signals.
focusKeyword: how to tell if a source is credible
content:
That is why checking credibility by staring harder at the page itself is often the wrong move.

Use lateral reading

Researchers at Stanford found that professional fact-checkers were faster and more accurate than historians and college students at evaluating unfamiliar websites. One important difference was their use of lateral reading: instead of staying on the original site, fact-checkers quickly opened other sources to understand who was behind it and what independent sources said about it.

This gives you a useful rule: when you do not know a source, leave the source.

1. Identify who is actually behind the page

Look for the author, organization, publication, and funding or ownership where relevant. Then search those names separately. Do not rely only on the source’s own About page. Ask what other credible organizations say about them.

2. Trace important claims to the original source

If an article says ‘a study found that 70% of people...’ click through. Did the study actually say that? Was it a peer-reviewed paper, a company survey, a press release, or another article repeating somebody else?

The more important the claim is to your decision, paper, or argument, the closer you should get to the primary evidence.

3. Separate expertise from confidence

A confident writing style is not evidence. Ask whether the author has relevant expertise for this specific claim. A physician may be credible on a clinical topic but not automatically on economics. A famous founder may have useful experience without being a reliable source for population-level research.

4. Check date and context

Some information ages slowly; other information expires quickly. A ten-year-old explanation of a mathematical theorem may be fine. A ten-year-old article about visa rules, software features, market prices, or medical guidance may be dangerously outdated.

5. Look for independent convergence

Do other credible sources reach the same conclusion? Agreement does not prove truth, but independent confirmation makes it harder for one misleading source to dominate your view.

6. Do not confuse citation density with credibility

A source can cite real research badly. Check whether key references support the sentence they are attached to. For high-stakes research, open the original study, inspect the methods and population, and see whether the result has been generalized beyond what was actually tested.

Build a small evidence trail

For serious work, save the sources you trust together with short notes on what each one supports. A reference manager works well for academic papers. A digital library can be useful when the evidence includes mixed formats such as reports, videos, official pages, datasets, and PDFs. If you use Kahana or any similar tool, the value is not simply storing links; it is preserving the context around why each source belongs in the collection.

Credibility is rarely a single badge you can spot on a page. It is a conclusion you reach by checking provenance, evidence, expertise, date, and independent context.
